“Jonah?” she said aloud. She didn’t know why she had spoken, but he stopped at once and waited.
She followed him down the steps and then down the short hill. They walked side by side. Her mind was still stuck on the Late Session, and she thought of nothing else. The others in their group had found each other attractive or repulsive. The observers had analyzed the body-language and verbal cues. Jonah had been silent: he always was, when she needed him.
text:
They started at Fulcrum’s front steps, an instant after the last of the lab staff had gone indoors and locked up. Mara’s mouth felt raw and dry; her throat ached, and her shoulders were rigid and aching too. Her entire body was too hot despite the cold, and she didn’t feel the chill of the night air.
The others were gone. Jonah stood silently beside her, waiting. He was six inches taller than she was. He wasn’t looking at her; his head turned toward the empty drive, and he stared into the darkness beyond the lighted entrance. There was nothing there. She didn’t look. She watched him instead.
“I guess it’s time to go home.” Jonah’s voice was soft, almost inaudible. She had expected more after tonight: analysis or commiseration. Instead he turned sideways with a small sigh and started down the front steps. He swung both arms easily, as though he were on an ordinary walk, though it was the middle of the night and they were both on their way back to hotel rooms in a town she didn’t know.

“Jonah?” she said aloud. She didn’t know why she had spoken, but he stopped at once and waited.
She followed him down the steps and then down the short hill. They walked side by side. Her mind was still stuck on the Late Session, and she thought of nothing else. The others in their group had found each other attractive or repulsive. The observers had analyzed the body-language and verbal cues. Jonah had been silent: he always was, when she needed him.

spark:
She followed.
They were walking out of town without talking. Her legs hurt, but Jonah’s stride was long and even; he kept picking up speed. She glanced over at him and saw that he looked tired, but there was something different too. He walked like a boy, shoulders thrown back, head lifted. He breathed loudly through his nose with every other step, then softly with the next two—three in and out, three, four, five.

spark:
He paused at the bottom step and looked back; his eyes were dark but his face wasn’t cold or angry or contemptuous. His gaze passed over her but he didn’t see her.
“Mara?”
His mouth opened and closed, but no sound came out.
“Do you—do you need a ride?”
“No.” She could feel her jaw moving. “Thanks.” Her feet came down too hard on the uneven bricks, and her shoulders hunched reflexively as she walked. She didn’t like the feel of the damp grass or the bumpy sidewalks under her heels. She didn’t know where Jonah was going; she didn’t need to know. There was a hotel about four blocks away, she had a map to it, she could walk there on her own. She didn’t need anyone’s help tonight or any other time.

She had stayed at Fulcrum all day without sleeping; she hadn’t planned to be here this late.
Mara glanced into the dark garage, where she had left her rental car in the afternoon, then followed him slowly, taking care not to touch his arm, which swayed close to hers with every other step.
